title: Logging Basics
description: Understand logging in ASP.NET Core Web API.

data.text: **Logging** is essential for monitoring, debugging, and diagnosing issues in production applications. ASP.NET Core ships with a built-in logging abstraction that lets you plug in providers such as Console, Debug, EventSource, and third-party sinks like Serilog, NLog, or Seq without changing your application code.

data.title: Why logging matters
data.text: Logs are usually the first place you look when something goes wrong in production. Choose a log level and message format that helps you (and your future self) understand *what happened*, *when*, and *why*.
How logging works in ASP.NET Core

The framework provides an `ILoggerFactory` that creates `ILogger<TCategory>` instances. When you request an `ILogger<MyService>`, the category name is automatically set to `MyService`, which makes filtering by area of the application trivial.

data.title: Injecting and using ILogger<T>
data.content: Inject ILogger<TCategory> into a controller and log at appropriate levels.

data.title: Always pass the exception object
data.text: Use the `LogError(exception, message)` overload so the full stack trace is captured. Never stringify an exception into a message — you lose the type, stack, and inner exceptions.

cards.title: LogInformation("User {UserId} did {Action}", id, action)
cards.description: Structured message template with named placeholders.

data.title: Registering providers in Program.cs
data.content: Add or remove logging providers at startup.

items.text: Pick a default minimum level (Information for production, Debug for development).
Add a structured sink (Console JSON, Seq, Application Insights, etc.).
Always pass the Exception object to LogError / LogCritical.
Avoid logging secrets, passwords, or full credit-card numbers.
Use request-scoped correlation IDs to trace a single request through your API.

data.title: Add logging to a CRUD endpoint
data.description: Practice adding structured logging to an existing ASP.NET Core Web API endpoint.
steps: Create a new controller `ProductsController` with a GET / POST / DELETE action.
Log an Information message when each action starts, including the product id.
Wrap the DELETE action in a try/catch and use `LogError(ex, ...)` on failure.
Run the API, hit each endpoint, and verify the messages appear in the console.
data.expectedOutcome: You should see distinct log lines per request with the correct level and category, and any exception should include a full stack trace.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use ILogger<T> for structured, category-scoped logging.
Choose the right severity — Information for normal flow, Warning/Error for trouble.
Always pass the Exception object instead of stringifying it.
Plug in providers via builder.Logging in Program.cs.
Avoid logging secrets or sensitive personal data.
data.takeaway: Good logging saves hours of debugging and is the foundation of observable services.
